images.alt: A Sinclair ZX Spectrum 48K computer with its grey rubber keyboard, photographed from above
images.caption: The ZX Spectrum, launched 23 April 1982, kept Sinclair's one-key-one-keyword BASIC but added colour, sound, and forty rubber keys.
images.author: Bill Bertram

images.alt: A Sinclair ZX Spectrum 48K computer viewed from the front, showing its black case and grey rubber keyboard
images.caption: A single Ferranti uncommitted logic array replaced most of the board a machine like this would otherwise have needed, and gave the Spectrum its price and its personality.
images.author: Jzh2074

images.alt: A Sinclair ZX Spectrum 48K with its metal keyboard template removed, exposing the single-piece bluish-grey rubber key mat underneath
images.caption: Steve Vickers' tokenising BASIC spared the rubber keyboard from constant use by making one keypress enter a whole command — PRINT, GO TO, RUN — rather than a single letter.
images.author: Multicherry

images.alt: A Sinclair ZX Spectrum 48K computer photographed at an angle, showing its rainbow stripe logo and rubber keyboard
images.caption: The rainbow stripe below the keyboard advertised the Spectrum's colour display, a first for a Sinclair computer.
images.author: Marcin Wichary from San Francisco, Calif.

images.alt: A Sinclair ZX Spectrum 48K computer, shown close up with its keyboard and edge connector visible
images.caption: Attribute clash — two moving objects forced to share the ink and paper colour of an 8×8 pixel block — became the Spectrum's most recognisable visual signature.
images.author: ccwoodcock
